name: Choi Bar
keyCorrections: If they pull their arm free, your shoulder clamp was loose — tighten the clamp before re-attacking.
If you can't find the armbar angle, your hip rotation is insufficient — turn your hips further away.
If they stack you, release the Choi bar and reset — don't fight the stack.
description: Use a shoulder clamp and wrist control from guard to move into an armbar line — a hybrid armbar that attacks from a 45-degree angle rather than the traditional perpendicular finish.
shortInstruction: Clamp the shoulder, control the wrist, rotate to the armbar line — the Choi bar finishes from an angle, not straight on.
summary: The Choi bar is a no-gi armbar variation that attacks from a 45-degree angle rather than the traditional perpendicular finish. You use a shoulder clamp (similar to the clamp guard) to trap their arm and shoulder, then rotate your hips to expose their elbow. The name comes from a combination of 'choke' and 'armbar' — it can be entered from choke setups and chains directly into the armbar. It is especially effective from the Kimura trap and clamp guard positions.
whyItWorks: The 45-degree angle of attack catches opponents who are used to defending the traditional 90-degree armbar.
The shoulder clamp prevents them from pulling their arm free — their elbow is exposed by your hip rotation.
It can be entered from common positions (guard, half guard, Kimura trap) without complex setup.
Danaher principle: attack the elbow from the angle they are not defending.
commonMistakes: Not controlling the shoulder before attacking the arm — the shoulder clamp must be tight.
Letting the opponent turn their elbow down — keep their palm facing up throughout.
Falling backward to finish instead of rotating the hips — the Choi bar uses hip rotation, not back fall.
Losing wrist control during the rotation — maintain the wrist grip as you rotate.
coachingCues: Clamp the shoulder, own the arm.
Rotate your hips, don't fall backward.
If they defend the Kimura, hit the Choi bar.
Palm up, elbow exposed, finish clean.
safetySummary: The Choi bar hyperextends the elbow — apply with control and release on tap.
Do not rotate explosively if you feel resistance at the elbow — a controlled finish prevents injury.
Never apply the armbar with sudden force — hyperextension injuries happen fast.

systemLogic.corePrinciple: Kimura trap or clamp guard: shoulder clamp → wrist control → rotate hips → expose elbow → extend for armbar.

decisionTree.action: The Choi bar works as a chain from the Kimura: if they defend the Kimura by hiding their arm, the Choi bar is the answer.
After the Choi bar, chain to Kimura or omoplata if they defend.

moneyDetails: The shoulder clamp is your foundation: one arm over their shoulder, the other controlling their wrist.
Rotate your hips away from them while pulling their wrist toward you — this exposes the elbow.
Keep their palm facing upward (supinated) throughout — a turned palm means the elbow is protected.
The finish is a short-range extension — you don't need to fully extend; just lift your hips and pull their wrist.
nextStep: After the Choi bar, learn the Kimura system and clamp guard control.
fixItFast: Can't rotate? Your hips are stuck — lift and turn, don't just pull the arm.
Arm keeps straightening? Palm must be up — rotate their wrist to supinate the arm.
They stack you? Release, frame on their hips, and reset to guard.
